core.text: After a comparative you can drop *quam* (than) and put the thing compared in the ablative: **the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he)**. *Canis lupō ferōcior est* — the dog is fiercer than a wolf; *nihil melle dulcius est* — nothing is sweeter than honey. The ablative usually stands right before the comparative. Latin name: *ablātīvus comparātiōnis*.
*Than* in English introduces the second half of a comparison: *braver than he*. Latin can leave the word out and let the case say it.
Comparative + ablative = 'than …'. With quam the two things are in the same case: *canis ferōcior est quam lupus*.

Two ablatives can sit around one comparative: *multō māior frātre* — bigger than his brother by much. The person is the ablative of comparison; **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multo maior = bigger by much)** is the measure (*multō, paulō, nihilō*).

more.text: The learner's notes (week 24) give *hic illō fortior est*, *haec illīs meliōra sunt*, *nihil hōc peius esse potest*. Ørberg glosses it in cap. XXIV: *melior frātre meō = melior quam frāter meus*; *stultior vōbīs = stultior quam vōs*.

The ablative is used only when the first thing compared is nominative or accusative; otherwise Latin keeps *quam*. It is the normal choice after negatives and in set phrases: *lūce clārius* (clearer than daylight), *opīniōne celerius* (faster than expected), *plūs aequō* (more than fair). Comparative adverbs take it too: *ventō celerius* — faster than the wind.
